picked.body: The third most visited country in Southeast Asia after Malaysia and Thailand welcomed nearly 16 million international visitors in the first eight months of 2026, up 14.4% year-on-year, driving up demand across hotels, travel companies, transport, restaurants and tourist attractions. A 2026 survey by Hoteljob.vn found that nearly 90% of tourism businesses planned to recruit. In Ho Chi Minh City alone, 89.7% of businesses were hiring, while 71.8% said recruitment was difficult or very difficult. The biggest shortages were among frontline workers, particularly in housekeeping, engineering, food service, front-office operations, and kitchens. The Politburo's Resolution dated Aug. 22, along with the government's action programme adopted on Sept. 7, set the target for tourism to directly contribute 10-12% of GDP by 2030, attracting 45-50 million international visitors and generate total revenue of US$80-90 billion. Hanoi, Ho Chi Minh City, and Da Nang are envisioned as major tourism growth hubs, while Phu Quoc emerges as a new hub. These targets will place greater demands on the tourism workforce, not only in terms of numbers but also skills, from frontline workers and foreign-language guides to managers, technology specialists and professionals delivering high-end services. Ho Chi Minh City's tourism sector, for example, is facing gaps in supervisory and management positions, as businesses seek staff capable of operating in an increasingly digitalized, international and competitive environment. Foreign-language tour guides are another weak link. Demand is rising rapidly from markets such as Russia and India, while arrivals from Europe and the Middle East are also increasing. Yet training guides with the language skills and cultural knowledge needed to serve these markets can take years. The labor crunch is even more acute in destinations far from major urban centers. In Con Dao, hotels and resorts regularly struggle to recruit receptionists, housekeepers, chefs, and service staff, while travel companies face shortages of sales, marketing, and tour guide staff. Higher salaries have done little to solve the problem. The island's high cost of living and distance from the mainland make it difficult to attract and retain skilled workers, with many leaving after only a few months. According to Hoteljob.vn, 79.5% of tourism businesses have raised salaries or improved benefits over the past year. Yet 59.2% cited lower incomes compared with other industries as a key reason young people leave the profession, while limited career prospects were another major factor. Experts say Vietnam's tourism labor shortage is not simply about training more people. The bigger challenge is narrowing the gap between what schools teach and what employers need. Nearly 80% of businesses surveyed said fewer than 20% of young applicants could start work immediately, while more than 84% said new recruits needed at least a month before they could work independently. Employers are also increasingly concerned with workplace discipline, service mindset and the ability to work under pressure, rather than technical skills alone. Experts say stronger links with policymakers, training institutions and businesses are needed to better forecast demand, redesign training and give young workers clearer career paths. Vietnam's tourism goals will require a workforce to match. If training and retention continue to lag behind visitor growth, the industry's labor shortage could become one of its biggest bottlenecks on the road to 2030.

picked.t: Man killed in HCMC after falling tree branch crushes motorbike during thunderstorm
picked.body: Le Van Dung and his wife, 57-year-old Duong Thi Thoan, were heading home from work along An Duong Vuong Street at around 6:30 p.m. when the tragedy struck. As they passed the Ho Chi Minh City University of Education in Cho Quan Ward, a massive tree branch broke in the strong winds and heavy rain , striking their vehicle and throwing them onto the road. The fallen branch, measuring approximately 30 cm in diameter, brought down a canopy large enough to completely block one traffic lane. The couple was transported to An Binh Hospital, about 1.2 km from the scene. Dung succumbed to his severe injuries shortly after arrival. Cho Quan Ward Chairman Nguyen Vo Xuan Ky confirmed that the wife sustained spinal trauma alongside multiple other injuries. She was later transferred to Cho Ray Hospital for treatment. Local authorities have visited the hospital to offer support to her and her family, he said, adding that the ward will formally request the local tree management agency to urgently inspect the area's canopy to prevent further tragedies. Prior to the recent expansion of HCMC's administrative boundaries to include Binh Duong and Vung Tau, official statistics recorded more than 200,000 trees lining over 1,200 city roads. Roughly 7,600 of these trees stand 20 to 50 meters tall, primarily concentrated in central districts. Many are decades-old dipterocarp and Hopea trees, distinguished by their large trunks and heavy branches, which pose a significant risk of breaking or uprooting during severe weather. An Duong Vuong Street is heavily shaded by these towering old-growth dipterocarps, known for their straight trunks and dense, year-round green foliage. However, the thoroughfare has a deadly track record regarding falling debris. In September 2024, a 20-cm-thick dipterocarp branch fell from nearly 20 m near the same university, killing a 52-year-old woman. Eight years earlier, in 2016, a dipterocarp measuring over 30 m tall and a meter in diameter was uprooted during heavy rain on the street, crushing a 25-year-old man who later died from his injuries.

picked.t: Patients pack Ho Chi Minh City's largest hospital from dawn as daily visits top 10,000
picked.body: Patients wait to see doctors at Cho Ray Hospital on Sept. 15. Reception counters at the hospital, the largest in southern Vietnam, begin issuing queue numbers at 4:30 a.m., leaving waiting halls packed before doctors started consultations at 6 a.m. Patient volumes at the hospital have jumped sharply since the beginning of this month. Dr. Le Trung Nhan, head of the Outpatient Department, said the facility typically receives 8,000 to 9,000 patient visits per day, with figures exceeding 10,000 on some days such as Sept. 7. Automatic ticket kiosks and reception counters remain heavily frequented, though conditions have eased over the past year following the introduction of an app-based appointment registration system that cuts down on early morning queues. More than 70% of patients now schedule visits in advance via the app, requiring them only to print their queue numbers upon arrival before heading straight to consultation rooms. To help manage the flow, personnel from the hospital's Social Work Department and a team of volunteers, primarily university students, deploy early each morning to guide and support arriving patients. This sustained influx is largely fueled by individuals requiring routine check-ups for chronic illnesses, cancer, cardiovascular diseases, and organ transplants. Overall, follow-up examinations account for roughly 60% of all patient traffic. With seating rows completely filled, 65-year-old Thu leaned against a pillar waiting for her turn outside the examination room after an early morning arrival. She reached the hospital at 5 a.m. following a more than four-hour bus journey from Bao Loc in Lam Dong Province near Da Lat, to HCMC. Thu had been experiencing persistent headaches, lightheadedness, dizziness, and numbness in both legs for several months. When local treatment in her hometown yielded no improvement after more than a month, she decided to seek medical attention at Cho Ray, where physicians ordered blood tests, an ultrasound, and a CT scan. picked.t: Central Group, controlled by Thai billionaire family Chirathivat, mulls $1.5B Vietnam investment
picked.body: "This is a particularly important market for us," Wallaya Chirathivat, chairwoman of Central Group, said during a press briefing on Thursday. Central Group entered Vietnam through Central Retail in 2012, and owns a range of retail brands, including GO!, Tops Market, Lan Chi Mart, and Supersports. It currently has 330 stores and shopping malls in 26 provinces and cities. It has invested $1.5 billion in Vietnam so far. Its plans to double that investment is driven by three main factors, the first being the country's rapid economic growth with GDP growing at 8-10% annually, outperforming the regional average, according to Chirathivat. Vietnam's population has surpassed 100 million, much larger than Thailand's, with consumers willing to shop through modern retail channels, she added. The economy also has a broad geographic structure stretching all the way from north to south, offering room for development across provinces and cities, she said. "We have cooperation agreements with Sun Group and other local businesses to research and develop projects," she said, referring to one of Vietnam's leading resort developers known for building landmarks and theme parks. Olivier Langlet, CEO of Central Retail Vietnam, said the investment plan would focus primarily on retail and shopping malls along with hotels. The company has identified 200 locations in urban areas for further study, he said. "Our team is very busy looking for suitable locations and land plots to develop projects. This is a very large workload." In the hotel business, in addition to the 984-room Centara Mirage Resort Mui Ne in Lam Dong, which has been operating since 2020, the company is developing two more properties in China-bordering Quang Ninh city, which will add about 1,000 rooms. Langlet said one challenge facing the proposal is that land in Vietnam has become "very expensive," requiring the company to carefully calculate its investments to ensure returns meet shareholders' expectations. Besides, while Vietnam has greatly simplified administrative procedures, it needs further improvements since some regulations remain ambiguous, making it difficult for investors to navigate through them. Central Retail's revenues in Vietnam in the first half of the year were more than 24 billion Thai baht (US$722 million), according to its financial report. This accounted for 20% of the company's overall revenues, making Vietnam its second largest market after Thailand. The Chirathivat family ranked fourth in Thailand's 50 Richest list compiled by Forbes this year. It has been in the list for nine years in a row.

picked.t: 4 Vietnamese restaurants removed from Tripadvisor list of Asia's best fine-dining
picked.body: They are The Soul Restaurant in the ancient town of Hoi An, November Restaurant & Sky Bar and Khue Restaurant in Hanoi, and Lai Restaurant in Ho Chi Minh City. Vietnam had five restaurants on the list last year . Among them, only the Rhythms Restaurant, located on the seventh floor of La Sinfonía del Rey Hotel & Spa in downtown Hanoi, stays on this year's list, ranking second behind Koma Singapore in the Travelers' Choice "Best of the Best" Restaurants Awards. The restaurant serves traditional Vietnamese dishes, including signature offerings such as roasted chicken prepared in the style of northwestern Vietnam, spring rolls and banana rolls served with ice cream. Another Vietnamese resprentative on the 2026 list was Reflections Restaurant inside Ho Chi Minh City's Caravelle Hotel, which finished the top 25. The HCMC restaurant serves international and European dishes amid a cosmopolitan setting with views of Lam Son Square and the Saigon Opera House. The 2026 Best of the Best Restaurants are calculated based on reviews and ratings for restaurants on Tripadvisor collected over a 12-month period, from July 1, 2025 through June 30, 2026 as well as an editorial process. The Travelers' Choice Awards Best of the Best title is awarded to those who receive a high volume of above-and-beyond reviews and opinions from the Tripadvisor community. Out of 8 million listings, fewer than 1% achieve this, according to the travel site.

picked.t: 25-year-old restaurant chain Crystal Jade closes 3 Singapore outlets in one month, 5 so far this year
picked.body: Crystal Jade recently confirmed to The Straits Times that its Hong Kong Kitchen outlet at The Clementi Mall had closed on Tuesday while its Jurong Point location is set to cease operations on Friday as part of its ongoing outlet network review. The group had closed another local outlet at the Great World shopping mall on Sept. 1 and two others earlier this year, citing the same reason, as reported by AsiaOne . Established in Singapore in 1991, Crystal Jade grew over the years and opened more than 100 outlets globally across several dining concepts in Singapore and overseas markets, including China, South Korea and Vietnam. Its operations in the city-state comprise six restaurant brands, ranging from Cantonese fine dining to casual noodle, dim sum and other Chinese cuisine concepts. Its Crystal Jade Golden Palace outlet at The Paragon mall was awarded one Michelin star from 2016 to 2018. Following the latest closures, Crystal Jade has 13 Singapore outlets, including four Hong Kong Kitchen restaurants, according to its website. The shutdowns add to the growing list of food and beverage closures in Singapore this year, with 2,101 such businesses shutting down in the first seven months, a 25.1% year-on-year increase, according to data from the Accounting and Corporate Regulatory Authority. Data released by the Singapore Department of Statistics earlier this month shows F&B services sales fell 1.9% year-on-year to an estimated S$1.6 billion in July, following a 2.3% decline in June. Food courts and other eating places, as well as cafes, saw the biggest declines of 6.6% and 6.4%, respectively, while fast-food outlets and food caterers reported sales growth.

picked.t: Tech workers spiral into anxiety, exhaustion because of 'age 35 curse'
picked.body: With no family dependents or debt to speak of, the Ho Chi Minh City programmer has nevertheless driven himself to total exhaustion for nearly two years. Beyond regular business hours, he works as a freelancer, taking on web design and software outsourcing contracts for clients across various time zones, leaving his desk strewn with half-eaten takeout containers and empty soda cans. "Every time a tech firm announces layoffs driven by automation, a chill runs down my spine," he says. Vietnamese tech workers are facing growing anxiety and burnout as layoffs, artificial intelligence and the industry's "age 35 curse" intensify pressure to keep working and upgrading their skills. Facing that same fear of obsolescence, Hoang Nam, a 34-year-old security engineer based in the southern province of Tay Ninh, also has a mortgage of over VND1 billion (US$40,000) and two young children. His company recently restructured, cutting nearly 20% of junior programming roles and replacing humans with automated coding tools. To safeguard his job, Nam took on extra in-house responsibilities while staying up late for freelance projects and teaching himself new machine learning tools. But after spending 15 hours a day staring at screens, his blood pressure consistently hovers above 140/90 mmHg. "Catching my reflection in the mirror at 3:00 a.m., with sunken eyes and a pounding heart, I know full well I'm destroying my body," Nam says. "But stopping now means losing my income and being replaced overnight by fresh graduates and younger coders." Terrified by the looming threat of a stroke, he checked into a hospital and was diagnosed with dyslipidemia, hypertension, prediabetes, and mild depression, all requiring long-term medical treatment. While nationwide figures remain unrecorded, the ordeal shared by Vinh and Nam dominates conversations across Vietnamese online tech communities. A persistent wave of layoffs in the industry, compounded by a desperate race to master emerging tools like AI is pushing software developers into chronic burnout. Clinicians are seeing the fallout firsthand. Medical professionals caution that the cohort of tech workers seeking treatment for chronic insomnia, physical collapse, and metabolic disorders is skewing dramatically younger. In its International Classification of Diseases (ICD-11), the World Health Organization defines burnout as an occupational syndrome resulting from chronic workplace stress that has not been successfully managed. The condition is marked by three core dimensions: energy depletion, growing mental detachment or cynicism toward one's job, and a steep decline in professional efficacy. Hoang Tien Trong Nghia, head of the neurology department at Ho Chi Minh City-based Military Hospital 175, says relentless stress triggers systemic inflammation and autonomic nervous dysfunction, significantly elevating the risk of cardiovascular disease, atherosclerosis, and strokes among younger adults. "Clinical practice has recently seen a surge in cases of hypertension, cardiac arrhythmia, and nervous breakdowns in patients under 35. "Nearly all of them have the same habits: hours of sedentary screen time, heavy reliance on stimulants like caffeine to pull all-nighters, and working under constant anxiety." Compounding this physical toll is a longstanding industry dread across Asian tech markets known as the "age 35 curse," or older professionals being stereotyped as slow to adapt, overly expensive due to seniority, and unable to keep pace with brutal overtime hours accepted by their younger colleagues. A 2024 tech recruitment survey by platform TopDev found that nearly 70% of Vietnamese tech companies prefer hiring engineers under 30 for frontline development roles to rein in payroll costs and maintain operational agility. That has only intensified as generative AI sweeps the tech landscape. Global layoff tracker Layoffs.fyi counted over 150,000 tech job cuts worldwide over the past year, heavily hitting baseline programming and quality assurance testing, tasks that automated algorithms can easily perform. Yet, from an employer's perspective, this weeding-out process is not merely about a number on a birth certificate. Nguyen Tuan Anh, chief technology officer at a Ho Chi Minh City software firm, argues that companies do not let people go simply because they turned 35, but rather because they "stopped delivering new value." Many professionals confuse a decade of growth with a single year of experience repeated 10 times over. As AI slashes the time needed to churn out routine code, businesses are trimming those who work mechanically, while holding on to talent that can untangle complex problems, design system architecture, and lead project delivery. "If a senior engineer cannot deliver markedly more value than a junior developer equipped with AI, they will inevitably face replacement," Anh points out. picked.t: Pressure to own home, car before marriage takes toll on young Vietnamese
picked.body: Minh, 32, a design professional in Tay Ninh Province, vividly remembers the night in mid-August when his body first rebelled. At about 3 a.m., he jolted awake with his heart pounding, his breathing short and shallow and his palms drenched in sweat. He sat on the edge of the bed until his heart rate slowed, returned to his computer, and resumed an unfinished design project. Three years earlier, he had set himself a goal of saving VND1.5 billion ($57,500) for an apartment down payment after relatives on both sides repeatedly told him, "A man should have a home in his own name before getting married." He spent 14 to 16 hours a day in front of a screen, taking on freelance projects outside his regular working hours, eating out and relying on strong coffee and energy drinks to stay awake. He gradually lost weight. The muscles in his neck, shoulders and jaw grew so tense that he repeatedly rolled his neck while he worked. After the first time, the nighttime palpitations returned several times a week. Alarmed, he headed for the University Medical Center Ho Chi Minh City, where he was diagnosed with an anxiety disorder requiring treatment. Hoang Quoc Lan, a mental health specialist at Phuong Dong General Hospital, described a similar case involving a 33-year-old Hanoi man. His relatives pressured him to marry whenever he returned to his hometown. The pressure was especially intense because they considered him responsible for carrying on the family line, as his household traditionally headed the extended family. Although he had a stable job, he did not feel financially established enough to marry because he owned neither a home nor a car and did not earn as much as his family expected. Fear of being judged led him to visit his hometown less often, avoid family gatherings, withdraw from friends and devote all his time to working and saving for a home. He gradually developed insomnia, frequent heart palpitations, a persistent sense of emptiness and loss of appetite. Lan diagnosed him with an anxiety disorder. "During counseling, he said what troubled him was not being single, but feeling that others saw him as a failure," Lan said. Vuong Nguyen Toan Thien, clinical director of the Lumos Center for Psychological Counseling and Therapy, says the divide between young adults’ hopes of homeownership and their financial means is widening, but no nationwide data tracks stress caused specifically by pressure to own property before marriage. Average per capita income rose by 6.4% a year between 2014 and mid-2025, while housing prices were on the fast lane. A family earning the Vietnamese per capita income and setting aside a third of it would need about 80 years to buy a 70-square-meter, two-bedroom apartment at mid-2025 prices if all numbers remain unchanged. The soaring housing costs are also stretching the timetable that young adults once expected their lives to follow. About 20 million men and women aged 15 or older had never married in 2024, according to data from the General Statistics Office of Vietnam. The mean age at first marriage was 27.3 that year, the highest ever. Between 1999 and 2019, the mean rose by 1.1 years. But in just the next five years, it rose by another 2.1. In some metropolises, the mean has now passed 30. Sociology describes the trend as "life-milestone inflation": Earning a degree, securing a stable job and finding a permanent home all take longer, making marriage feel like a luxury that must be pushed farther down the list. Citing a 2024 review of research on financial stress, Thien says prolonged financial strain can affect the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis, or HPA axis, and activate the sympathetic nervous system, increasing the release of cortisol and adrenaline. When people push themselves beyond their limits in a race to accumulate assets, the body’s alarm system can remain stuck in the "on" position, he says. Persistently elevated cortisol levels can interfere with the body’s melatonin cycle and disrupt deep sleep. Insufficient deep sleep also hinders the brain’s glymphatic system, which is involved in removing metabolic waste, potentially contributing to brain fog, memory problems, and what Thien describes as "cellular energy depletion." Prolonged activation of the sympathetic nervous system can also reduce heart rate variability, or HRV, a measure of the cardiovascular system’s ability to recover and adapt, he says. Low HRV has been associated with elevated markers of systemic inflammation, including C-reactive protein, or CRP, and pro-inflammatory cytokines. Thien says these stress-related changes may raise the risk of early cardiovascular disease, irritable bowel syndrome, tension-type headaches, and weakened immune function in young workers. Social expectations surrounding gender can also shape how people respond to pressure over assets before marriage, though individual responses vary widely, he says. picked.t: World's second largest asset manager Vanguard to pour $2.5B into Vietnam stocks
picked.body: The fund is expected to be disbursed within a year, following the official upgrade of the stock market under FTSE Russell standards, said Duncan Burns, head of Investments and Global Equity for Asia-Pacific at Vanguard, at an event on Friday. This figure is higher than previous estimates by several Vietnamese analytical firms, which had projected between $1 billion and $2 billion. Burns added that markets included in major benchmark indices typically gain higher visibility, attracting investor participation and enhancing access to global capital. "Many investors may have never visited Vietnam, but through us, they can participate in the sustainable growth of this market," the Vanguard representative said. Vietnam's stock market will officially be upgraded to "emerging" status under FTSE Russell standards on Sept. 21. This will provide Vietnamese equities with greater opportunities to attract international investment capital. Vanguard funds tracking the FTSE Global Equity Index Series are expected to make net purchases of approximately $240.5 million across 27 Vietnamese stocks, according to calculations from stocker brokerage SSI Research. Founded in 1975, Vanguard is the second-largest asset management company in the world, trailing only BlackRock. The fund currently manages approximately $13 trillion in assets for more than 60 million investors worldwide. In FTSE's latest portfolio published at the end of August, 27 Vietnamese stocks were added to the organization's emerging market index basket. This global stock index series is designed to represent nearly the entire investable equity market worldwide. Broken down by market capitalization, three stocks were classified into the large-cap group: Vietcombank, Vingroup , and Vinhomes. In the mid-cap group, FTSE Russell added BIDV, Hoa Phat Group, and VPBank. The remaining 21 tickers belong to the small-cap group. Minister of Finance Ngo Van Tuan said Friday that regulatory agencies will continue to raise governance quality and market discipline. His ministry will lay the legal groundwork for new market models and products in line with modern market development trends. Tuan affirmed that the agency will continue reforms to build a transparent, safe, and attractive capital market. This effort aims to facilitate conditions for investors, especially foreign investors, and improve market access in accordance with international standards.

picked.t: Vietnamese student gives up Western plans to follow his sister to 'China's MIT'
picked.body: Nguyen Khoa Vu, a graduate of Hanoi's Foreign Language Specialized School, has won a 50% tuition scholarship to Tsinghua University's Zhishan College. Tsinghua, often dubbed "China's MIT", ranks 14th in the QS World University Rankings 2027. Zhishan, a social sciences college Tsinghua launched in 2024, charges CNY26,000 (US$3,900) a year in tuition. Its majors include economics, sociology, political science and public administration, international politics and statistics. Vu's older sister, Nguyen Vu Tue Giang, was admitted to Tsinghua on a scholarship in 2025. Used to Western culture and passionate about basketball, Vu flatly refused when his mother suggested he follow his sister to Beijing. "At one point I told my parents straight out: "either the U.K. or the U.S., or I stay home," he recalled. In August 2025, he traveled to Beijing with his family for his sister's enrollment. The modern classrooms, swimming pool and basketball courts, along with time spent with Vietnamese students there, won him over. "Everything felt right, and I realized this was the environment for me," he said. Vu's application included his transcripts, language certificates, recommendation letters, a personal essay and a self-introduction video. He also submitted math and Chinese results from the China Scholastic Competency Assessment (CSCA), a new standardized test for international undergraduate applicants. He kept an average above 9 out of 10 throughout high school. His language scores include IELTS 7.5 and HSK 6, the highest of the Chinese proficiency test's six core levels. In his essay, Vu wrote about setting aside his dream of playing professional basketball to focus on academics and economics. "I wanted to show that however passionate I am about sports, I can set it aside and excel at another goal," he said. "A sports career is a huge challenge because it requires substantial resources and the right environment to develop," he added. He picked economics because he inherited his mother's head for business, he said. While still in school, he imported trendy toys and sold sneakers online. After clearing the application review, Vu advanced to an in-person interview. Three professors spent 15 minutes questioning him on a range of topics and even had him solve math problems on the spot. Candidates must keep the interview content confidential. "At one point I admitted I didn't know anything about a topic the professor raised and asked for a different question," Vu said, crediting honesty for his success. Vu handled pressure remarkably well, moving from HSK 4 to HSK 6 in six months, said Hoang Lan Chi, a lecturer at Hanoi's University of Languages and International Studies who guided him through the application. "Vu proved he meets the university's admission criteria. He is well-rounded, from academics, music and sports to determination, perseverance and discipline," she said. Giang, self-motivated and a natural student, mostly needed support from the sidelines, said their mother, Mai Dung. Vu was capable but sometimes distracted, she said, so she watched him more closely, often pointing to successful role models and steering him toward his sister's example. "I let my children experience things, take responsibility and face failure early, while quietly creating situations that spark their passion," she said. She believes that bringing Vu along to his sister's enrollment, and letting him mingle with Tsinghua students, helped him find his own goal.
